justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I'd infer was a starting price around 314–315, with each horizon adding a small positive increment. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed level, expecting minimal drift and mean-reverting intraday noise to dominate. At one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to around 317, reflecting a mild bullish drift assumption consistent with broad equity index behavior over short horizons under normal conditions. At one month, I pushed to 320, incorporating a longer-run drift assumption while acknowledging that one month is long enough for meaningful macro developments to materially shift the level.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each horizon. For a one-day window, annualized volatility in the 15–20% range translates to daily moves of roughly 1–1.3%, giving a tight band around the point estimate. As the horizon extends to one week, the uncertainty grows with the square root of time, widening the band noticeably. At one month, the interval spans roughly plus or minus 11% around the point estimate, which is consistent with historical distributions of monthly returns for major equity indices or ETFs priced in this range. I also factored in that volatility tends to cluster, so if conditions were already elevated, I'd shade the intervals wider.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macro shocks — a surprise central bank policy shift, an unexpected inflation print, or a geopolitical escalation — any of which could produce moves well beyond the one-month band in a matter of days. On the upside, a strongly positive economic surprise or dovish policy pivot could drive a sharp rally that exceeds the upper bound. Liquidity events or technical breakdowns during low-volume periods could also generate outsized moves at the short end that breach the one-day interval.

Finally, my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, which underweight fat-tail events by construction. Real-world return distributions have excess kurtosis, meaning extreme outcomes occur more frequently than my stated 90% confidence intervals imply. Anyone relying on these forecasts should treat the tails as softer boundaries than the precise numbers suggest, particularly at the one-month horizon where structural uncertainty about the economic environment compounds the statistical uncertainty.
